summary: Mobile IPv6 bootstrapping has a split scenario, where network access and mobility service are authorized by different parties, and an integrated scenario, where one party authorizes both. This RFC defines how a mobile node finds home agent information in the integrated scenario.

eli5.summary: Sometimes one ticket office handles both your bus ride and your hotel. This memo explains how a traveler finds the hotel details when one office does both.

questions: how does mobile ipv6 bootstrapping work in the integrated scenario
how to find a home agent for mobile ipv6
what is the integrated scenario in mobile ipv6 bootstrapping
how does the nas pass home agent information to dhcp
what is the difference between split and integrated bootstrapping
subtitle: How a roaming Mobile IPv6 node finds its home agent when one operator handles both access and mobility.

tldr.problem: A Mobile IPv6 node needs a home address, a home agent address and keying material, and must get them dynamically. In the integrated scenario one party authorizes both network access and mobility service.
tldr.mechanism: During network access authentication the home AAA server tells the NAS which home agent was assigned. The co-located DHCP relay passes that to the DHCP server in a Relay-Supplied Options option, and the server answers the node's DHCPv6 request using the options from RFC 6610.
tldr.outcome: The node learns its home agent from a DHCPv6 reply. If that fails, it may fall back to DNS-based discovery as defined in RFC 5026.

today: RFC 6611 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the DHCP options defined in RFC 6610.

sections.title: Bootstrapping Mobile IPv6
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 (RFC 6275) requires the mobile node to have a Home Address (HoA), a home agent address and cryptographic materials for an IPsec security association with the home agent. The mechanism for obtaining these is called Mobile IPv6 bootstrapping.

RFC 4640 sets out two scenarios. In the split scenario the entity that authorizes network access (the Access Service Authorizer, ASA) differs from the one that authorizes mobility service (the Mobility Service Authorizer, MSA), and RFC 5026 covers it. In the integrated scenario the ASA is also the MSA, and this RFC covers it.

RFC 5026 names four components of the problem: home agent address discovery, HoA assignment, IPsec security association setup, and authentication and authorization with the MSA. This document defines only the first. It works through DHCP and AAA, using the DHCP options of RFC 6610 and the AAA attribute-value pairs of RFC 5447.
sections.eli5: Getting ready to travel takes several steps. This memo covers just one: learning where your home helper lives, in the case where one office handles everything.

sections.title: Assumptions and Conformance
sections.content:
The document assumes that MSA and ASA are the same, that the MSA and the MSP have a roaming relationship, and that the DHCP relay and the NAS are either co-located or have a way to pass AAA information from the NAS to the relay. It also assumes the NAS supports the MIPv6-specific AAA attributes of RFC 5447, and that the home AAA server (AAAH) used for access authentication has access to the same database as the one used for mobility authentication.

If a deployment needs home agent assignment only in the access network (ASP), a minimal implementation MAY support only delivery from the DHCP server to the client as in RFC 6610. If assignment in the mobility provider's network (MSP) is needed, a conforming implementation SHALL be able to pass AAA information from the AAA server to the NAS and from the NAS to the DHCP relay. The interface between those functions is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The plan only works if the front desk and the helper who answers questions can talk to each other, either because they sit together or share a phone line.

sections.title: The Integrated Scenario
sections.content:
The mobile node uses its network access authentication to bootstrap Mobile IPv6. The access service authorizer is assumed to be mobility service aware. The mechanism requires the NAS to support MIP6-specific AAA attributes and a co-located DHCP relay agent.

The AAA infrastructure has a AAA client (the NAS), a AAA proxy in the visited network (AAAV) and a AAA server in the home network (AAAH). The user's home network authorizes the node for both access and mobility. The home agent may be selected in the access provider's network or in the mobility provider's network, and the MSP may be co-located with the ASP or the ASA/MSA, or be independent of both.

The mobile node talks to the DHCP server through the relay agent after network access authentication, as part of its normal configuration.
sections.eli5: One office decides both whether you may ride the bus and whether you may use the hotel. The bus stop and the hotel can be run by that office or by other companies it trusts.

sections.title: The Bootstrapping Message Sequence
sections.content:
The same five steps describe both variants (Figure 2 in the RFC). In step 1 the node authenticates for network access (for example with IEEE 802.11i/802.1X) through the NAS, which talks to the AAAH. The AAAH checks in the AAA profile that the node may use Mobile IPv6, assigns a home agent in the home MSP and one or more in other authorized MSPs, and returns this to the NAS. The NAS may keep it for a configurable time, or as long as the node stays connected. In step 2 the node sends a DHCPv6 Information-request to the All_DHCP_Relay_Agents_and_Servers multicast address. In step 3 the relay forwards it to the DHCP server, with the AAA information in a Relay-Supplied Options option. In step 4 the server replies. In step 5 the relay passes the reply on, and the node has the home agent information.

Home agent in the MSP

The node's request lists the Visited Home Network Information option in its OPTION_ORO, includes a Client Home Network ID FQDN option identifying the MSP, and includes its OPTION_CLIENTID. The server identifies the client by its DUID, sees from the FQDN option that MSP information is wanted, sees from the Relay-Supplied Options option that the AAAH allocated the home agent, and returns that information in an Identified Home Network Information option. If the NAS does not store the information for the whole session and the node delays its DHCP request, the relay does not include the Relay-Supplied Options option.

Home agent in the ASP

Here the node asks for a home agent in the ASP by setting the id-type field to zero in its Home Network Identifier Option, and the ASP becomes the MSP for the duration of the access authentication session. The AAAH does not know the node prefers the ASP, so the home agent it assigned may go unused, which leaves the choice of mobility anchor to the node. If configured to do so, the DHCP server allocates a home agent from its own configured list and returns it in a Visited Home Network Information option, without using the Relay-Supplied Options content.
sections.eli5: The traveler shows ID at the front desk. The desk learns which hotel the traveler's company booked, and passes that note to the information clerk. When the traveler asks the clerk, the clerk reads it out.

sections.title: Fallback and Remaining Bootstrapping Steps
sections.content:
In the fallback case, the node cannot get home agent information through DHCPv6. It MAY then perform DNS queries to discover the home agent address as defined in RFC 5026. To do this it needs a DNS server address, and how it gets one is outside the scope of this document.

The other bootstrapping components, which are HoA assignment, IPsec security association setup and authentication and authorization with the MSA, are done in the integrated scenario by the same mechanism as in the split scenario of RFC 5026.
sections.eli5: If the clerk cannot help, the traveler can look the hotel up in the phone book instead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The assigned home agent information travels from the AAA server to the NAS over the AAA infrastructure, and may be only integrity protected by standard Diameter or other AAA security mechanisms. The security mechanisms of RFC 3588 apply. The RFC states that no additional security considerations come from using it, and that it introduces no new security issues to Mobile IPv6.
sections.eli5: The note passed between offices is protected the same way other office notes are, and nothing new is added.
